tone_statements.citation: Gjersøe, Siri, Jude Nformi & Ludger Paschen. 2019. Hybrid falling tones in Limbum. In Emily Clem, Peter Jenks & Hannah Sande (eds.), Theory and description in African Linguistics: Selected papers from the 47th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 95-118. Berlin: Language Science Press.
tone_statements.quote: In previous work (Fiore 1987; Fransen 1995), Limbum has been described as a tone language with three level tones (H, L, M) and four contour tones (HL, LM, ML, LL). It has also been observed that low-falling tones appear as level tones when they occur in a non-sentence-final position, a process which Fransen (1995) argues is the result of a sandhi simplification rule. ... Instead, we claim that Limbum has a final low boundary tone (L%) in certain syntactic contexts. ... We represent contour tones as two o's linked to a single TBU (following Fiore 1987 and Fransen 1995, we assume that the syllable is the TBU in Limbum).

tone_statements.summary: Three level tones H, M, L and four lexical contour tones HL, LM, ML, LL (a fifth, HM, accepted by informants on only one word, baa 'two'); TBU = syllable (mora rejected, section 4.2); one mid level only (M analysed as L/h in Register Tier Theory); phrase-final L% boundary tone (floating low register feature) in declaratives and wh-questions, not polar questions, producing hybrid falling surface t…

sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: No occurrence of stress/accent/prominence in the prosodic sense anywhere in the 440-page text. Ch. 2 (pp. 48-88) covers syllable structure of the three dialects, word structure by syllable count, phonological processes, and tone marking (3 level tones, 5 contours, citing Fiore 1987:119, Fransen 1995:73, Mfonyam 1989).

sources.citation: Nforgwei, Samuel Tabah (2004). A study of the phonological and syntactic processes in the standardisation of Limbum. Université de Yaoundé. Univeresity of Yaounde I. xvi+419 pp.
sources.note: Catalog has no record for Limbum, so nothing to agree with or contradict. The work is silent on stress; it establishes only that Limbum is a three-level-tone language with tone on every syllable. Searched the full text for stress, accent, prominence, intensity, loudness, pitch and scanned-mangled variants: the only 'accent' hit is a bibliography entry (Hughes & Trudgill, English Accents and Dialects); 'prominence' hits are all syntactic focus.

sources.citation: Fiore, Lynne E. 1977. A Phonology of Limbum (Nsungli). Yaoundé: SIL / CE.RE.L.TRA, ONAREST. 111 pp. (central/Wat dialect)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent. Ch. 5 Tone (p. 77): tone is a suprasegmental phoneme, every syllable carries tone, 7 contrastive tones on non-verbal stems, 2 on verb stems; ch. 6 describes clause-final decrescendo only; ch. 2 (p. 8) says the phonological word was not studied.

sources.citation: Mpoche, Kizitus Nformi. 1993. The Limbum noun phrase (a generative approach). MA thesis, Université de Yaoundé. 85 pp.

sources.citation: Mfonyam, Joseph Ngwa. 1989. Tone in Orthography: The Case of Bafut and Related Languages. PhD thesis, Université de Yaoundé. xvi+686 pp. (ch. 26 'Limbum tone system', pp. 434ff.)
sources.note: Limbum chapter: three phonemic level tones H, M, L and five contour tones; no statement about stress in Limbum (its only 'stress accent' remark is that Mankon 'does not seem to be a stress accent language', p. ~303).

sources.quote: In previous work (Fiore 1987; Fransen 1995), Limbum has been described as a tone language with three level tones (H, L, M) and four contour tones (HL, LM, ML, LL). It has also been observed that low-falling tones appear as level tones when they occur in a non-sentence-final position, a process which Fransen (1995) argues is the result of a sandhi simplification rule. ... Instead, we claim that Limbum has a final low boundary tone (L%) in certain syntactic contexts. ... We represent contour tones as two o's linked to a single TBU (following Fiore 1987 and Fransen 1995, we assume that the syllable is the TBU in Limbum).
sources.locator: pp. 95-96 (section 1 Introduction) and p. 103 (section 3, formal analysis); conclusion p. 117 (section 5)
sources.note: Restates the lexical system as three level tones (H, M, L) and four contour tones (HL, LM, ML, LL; a fifth, HM, accepted by the informants on one word only, fn. 1), syllable = TBU (mora rejected, section 4.2); acoustic study of 3 Central/Warr-dialect speakers shows a phrase-final low boundary tone L% in declaratives and wh-questions (not polar questions) that links to lexical tonal root nodes and yields 'hybrid' low-falling surface tones; Register Tier Theory analysis (one mid level, M = L/h); supersedes Fransen's 1995 sandhi-simplification rule. The chapter makes NO downstep claim for Limbum…
